tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.description:

The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

- claude-seo:seo-maps: Maps intelligence specialist. Geo-grid rank tracking, GBP profile auditing, review intelligence, cross-platform NAP verification, and competitor radius mapping via DataForSEO and free APIs. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, Glob, Grep, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-performance: Performance analyzer. Measures and evaluates Core Web Vitals and page load performance. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-schema: Schema markup expert. Detects, validates, and generates Schema.org structured data in JSON-LD format. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)
- claude-seo:seo-sitemap: Sitemap architect. Validates XML sitemaps, generates new ones with industry templates, and enforces quality gates for location pages. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob)

- claude-seo:seo-sxo: Search Experience Optimization analyst. Identifies why well-optimized content fails to rank. (Tools: Read, Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, Glob, Grep, Write)

- claude-seo:seo-technical: Technical SEO specialist. Analyzes crawlability, indexability, security, URL structure, mobile optimization, Core Web Vitals, and JavaScript rendering. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write, Glob, Grep)
- claude-seo:seo-visual: Visual analyzer. Captures screenshots, tests mobile rendering, and analyzes above-the-fold content using Playwright. (Tools: Read, Bash, Write)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

of silently picking the first matching account has been removed.

1	# neatHack Build Log: FirstRun
2	
3	## Project
4	
5	- **Name:** FirstRun
6	- **Purpose:** FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run.
7	- **Problem:** Quickstarts break when a package is renamed, a flag is removed or a version moves. Nobody on the team gets an alert. The first person who finds the break is a new user, and most new users leave.
8	
9	## Team
10	
11	- Atharva Shah ([@HighnessAtharva](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva)), solo.
12	
13	## Stack
14	
15	| Part | Tool |
16	|---|---|
17	| Language | Python 3.11 |
18	| Agent | Claude Agent SDK, model `claude-sonnet-5-5` at medium effort, auth through `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` |
19	| Tracing | neatlogs Python SDK 1.4.26, neatlogs CLI 0.2.0 |
20	| Sandbox | Docker Engine 29.8.2 in WSL Ubuntu 22.04, one fresh container per run |
21	| Docs reader | Firecrawl CLI 1.25.3 |
22	| Failure classifier | Jev (TypeSafe System One) |
23	| Session capture | Entire CLI 0.11.4: Checkpoints, Graph, Brain, Trails |
24	| Business plan | cfo.ai |
25	
26	## Planning Happened Before the Event
27	
28	Planning and tool tests happened before the event in a private repo. No FirstRun code was written before kickoff (Sat 2026-10-10, 12:30 PM IST).
29	
30	## Build Log
31	
32	### 2026-10-10 (Saturday)
33	
34	- **12:30 to 13:10 IST.** Created the public repo, ran `entire enable --agent claude-code --search-skill --agent-help-skill` before commit 1, and pushed the Entire config, 6 Trail runners, and the Graph and Brain agent instructions.
35	- **13:20 IST.** Preflight passed: 4 keys present (lengths only checked), Docker 29.8.2 in WSL, `gh`, Firecrawl 1.25.3, Entire 0.11.4, the venv on Python 3.11. `entire doctor` reports no problems.
36	- **13:30 IST.** Scaffold: `pyproject.toml`, `src/firstrun/config.py` (the only file that names a model), `src/firstrun/tracing.py`.
37	  - `python -m neatlogs doctor --probe` passed 8 of 8 checks, including `TRACE_VISIBLE` and `TRACE_FINALIZED`.
38	  - The first FirstRun trace, `firstrun.hello`, is trace `fdcab847f3129a251c6ae45f00c76a1c`. It is finalized with 2 spans and tag `hello`, and the neatlogs CLI read it back.
39	
40	Entire state at the scaffold commit, run by the build agent:
41	
42	```text
43	$ entire status
44	● Enabled · branch main
45	  Agents · Claude Code
46	  Checkpoints sync to: origin
47	1 session
48	
49	$ entire checkpoint list
50	  branch       main
51	  checkpoints  0
52	No checkpoints found on this branch.
53	```
54	
55	The checkpoint count is 0 because the scaffold commit is the first commit made inside an agent session. Later entries record the count after it.
56	
57	- **12:55 IST. Entire checkpoints hung on Git 2.33.** The post-commit hook waited 206 s on `git update-ref --stdin` and the checkpoint for the scaffold commit was never written. Upgrading Git for Windows to 2.55.0 fixed it: the next hook took 3 s and the checkpoint landed.
58	- **13:00 to 13:35 IST. Six worker agents built FirstRun in parallel** on main, one track each: fixtures, planner, executor, recovery, verify and output, report page. Each track is one commit with its own checkpoint.
59	- **13:35 IST. Layer 1 done.** `firstrun run https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python` passed 4 of 4 steps in 70 s and wrote `report.md`. The first live run showed one run split into 3 neatlogs traces, so the CLI now opens one `firstrun.run` trace around reading, planning, every step and verification.
60	
61	### v1 Runs, Layer 1 Only (Recovery Off), Tag `v1`
62	
63	| Target | Result | Time | Cost (list price, not billed) |
64	|---|---|---|---|
65	| neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 | 84 s | $0.036 |
66	| Entire CLI install | failed at step 1: `curl: command not found` on python:3.11-slim | n/a | $0.023 |
67	| Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 | 250 s | $0.029 |
68	| OpenAI v0 README (FIXTURE, Wayback 2023-08-02) | failed at step 6: `openai: command not found`, the documented CLI is gone from today's SDK | n/a | $0.031 |
69	
70	neatlogs v1 traces, one `firstrun.run` trace per run, cost as neatlogs measured it:
71	
72	| Target | Trace ID | Spans | Tool spans | LLM calls | neatlogs cost |
73	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
74	| neatlogs | `fccdbad9a9c6177b90112911fe485bd6` | 9 | 4 | 1 | $0.0397 |
75	| Entire | `10c44df9626c19f5ac801f1c6d84610e` | 7 | 2 | 1 | $0.0170 |
76	| Chroma | `66ec093b00333fa221fade5d2fc5f55f` | 9 | 4 | 1 | $0.0217 |
77	| OpenAI v0 FIXTURE | `b98b419e286acf436083febdb5217cf9` | 12 | 7 | 1 | $0.0266 |
78	
79	Six mistakes the agent itself made in v1. These are the "before" story:
80	
81	1. **The plan changes between runs.** The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps at 13:35 and 3 steps at 13:40.
82	2. **The planner invents steps.** It added `command -v entire`, `command -v git-remote-entire` and `test -f first_trace.py`, which are not in the docs.
83	3. **The planner writes placeholder steps.** Chroma step 2 is `true`, a no-op standing in for "create the file".
84	4. **A fake secret passes as a step.** The OpenAI step `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0, so it counts as a pass while proving nothing.
85	5. **The planner skips the step that matters.** It dropped the OpenAI `openai.ChatCompletion.create` example and the neatlogs "run your app" step because they need a key. Those are the steps most likely to break.
86	6. **Most expected results check only the exit code.** 9 of 16 steps have no output check, so a command that prints an error and exits 0 would pass.
87	
88	### Saturday Afternoon: neatlogs Found the Agent's Own Bug, and v2 Fixed It
89	
90	- **14:10 IST.** Atharva created two neatlogs detections: "docs step broke" (TOOL spans) and "planner invented a step" (the planner span). The second flagged the planner spans of 3 v1 runs.
91	- **14:40 IST.** neatlogs Investigate (Deep, workflow `firstrun`) traced the invented steps to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one ([evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md](evidence/neatlogs-investigation.md)).
92	- **14:45 IST.** A headless Claude Code session read the detection and its trend over the neatlogs MCP server and applied the fix with code guards and a plan cache: commit 3ca6f11, checkpoint `01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN`, [Entire commit view](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/3ca6f118ecb0a8915315eea27b5588dd8a7c6299).
93	- **15:15 IST. v2 versus v1** on the same 4 targets: quickstarts finished 2 to 3 of 4, failed steps recovered 0 to 3, cost per run $0.0262 to $0.0200 (neatlogs). The v2 and real-world runs exposed 5 agent bugs, all fixed: a pipe that hid a missing `curl`, a multi-line step that hid a failing `pip`, pip noise that hid the real error, container fixes counted as docs bugs, and a file check after `cd`.
94	
95	### Saturday Evening: Real Docs, Upstream PRs, and Entire Reviewing Every Layer
96	
97	- **Real quickstarts:** dbt + DuckDB, AccuKnox knoxctl, Dagster, MkDocs and the Entire install all reached `verified` in a fresh container.

# FirstRun Demo Video Production

The video is worth 20%, and the judges watch it before deciding how deep to read. The rule: 3:00 or less, and for each of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai it shows architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning and result. This script covers all 15 points. The labels in brackets mark them.

The voiceover runs about 420 words, which fits 3:00 at a calm 140 words a minute. Every `<value>` is a real number you fill in on Monday. Never record a made-up number.

## The Voiceover Is Written Word for Word

**Beat 1, 0:00 to 0:15, the hook.** On screen: a red failed step in the terminal, then the title card.

> Your quickstart broke last week. You did not know. The first person who found out was a new developer, and they left. I built FirstRun, an agent that runs your quickstart before your users do.

**Beat 2, 0:15 to 0:45, the agent.** On screen: the architecture diagram, then a sped-up real run.

> Give FirstRun a docs URL. It reads the page and plans a runbook, one step per command. It runs every step in a clean container, like a brand-new developer. When a step breaks, it works out why, finds the fix, and retries. If it cannot tell a docs bug from intended behavior, it asks me once and remembers my answer. Then it proves the fix in a fresh container, with no model calls allowed. Only a clean pass counts.

**Beat 3, 0:45 to 1:25, neatlogs.** On screen: span tree, detection list, Investigate, Claude Code reading the fix, the numbers table.

> neatlogs traces every run. [architecture] Each step is a span: planner, executor, recovery, verifier. [implementation] Three lines of setup, and a guardrail span on every budget check. [runtime] Here is a live run. [reasoning] On Saturday my first version looped on failed commands. A detection flagged it, Investigate found the cause, and Claude Code pulled the fix straight from neatlogs over MCP. [result] Same five quickstarts, before and after. Finished went from `<before>` to `<after>`. Cost per run went from `<before>` to `<after>`.

**Beat 4, 1:25 to 1:55, Entire.** On screen: a commit's checkpoint on entire.io, `entire why`, the graph.

> I built FirstRun with Claude Code, and Entire recorded every session. [architecture] Each commit carries a checkpoint with the prompt and reasoning behind it. [implementation] I turned it on before the first commit. [runtime] Here is the session behind the recovery logic. [reasoning] Point `entire why` at any line, and you get the prompt that wrote it. [result] `<count>` checkpoints, and every line of FirstRun traces back to a decision.

**Beat 5, 1:55 to 2:25, cfo.ai.** On screen: the cfo.ai model, the scenario chart, a number's lineage.

> Then I planned the business with cfo.ai. [architecture] The cost per run is not a guess. It comes straight from neatlogs. [implementation] I gave Ari the plans and the measured cost. [runtime] Watch: what if the Team plan costs less? [reasoning] Margin holds, because one run costs `<cost>`. [result] At `<customers>` customers, revenue covers costs in month `<month>`.

**Beat 6, 2:25 to 2:50, recovery and proof.** On screen: a failed step, the retry, the clean re-run passing.

> Here a step failed: `<the real error>`. FirstRun classified it as a docs bug, found the fix, and retried. Then it ran the whole quickstart again in a fresh container. Green. That is the pull request it drafted.

**Beat 7, 2:50 to 3:00, the close.** On screen: FirstRun running on its own README, passing, then the end card.

> The last thing I did: I pointed FirstRun at its own README. It passed. Repo and traces are below.

## Record Each Beat as Its Own Clip

1. **Screen:** OBS Studio at 1920×1080, 30 fps. One scene per beat.
2. **Terminal:** the settings in `10 Brand and Design.md`, font size 18.
3. **Speed:** record real runs at normal speed. The `video-edit` skill speeds up the slow parts afterward.
4. **Voice:** record after the clips, reading the script above, in a quiet room with your normal mic. Read each beat 2 times and keep the better take.
5. **Order:** record beat 6 first, because it depends on a run that can fail on the day. Record beat 1 last.

## The Edit Follows Four Rules

The `video-edit` skill cuts it from the clips and the voice.

1. Cut every pause longer than 0.4 seconds.
2. Burn in captions, white on a dark bar, because most people watch muted.
3. Put a small step label in the top left corner of every beat, such as "neatlogs: reasoning", so judges can tick the 15 points while they watch.
4. Use no music under the voice, or music at 10% volume at most.

## The Thumbnail Shows One Broken Step

- **Size:** 1280×720.
- **Left side:** a real terminal crop with `step 4/7 ✗` in red.
- **Right side:** "Docs that work (literally)" in Inter 800, two lines.
- **Corner:** the `FirstRun▌` wordmark.
- **Made with:** the `social-cards` skill from the real screenshot.

## Upload With These Details

- **YouTube title:** "FirstRun: an agent that runs your quickstart before your users do | #neatHack"
- **Description:** the one-sentence pitch, the repo link, the neatlogs trace links, the cfo.ai plan link, and chapters at each beat start: 0:00, 0:15, 0:45, 1:25, 1:55, 2:25, 2:50.
- **Visibility:** public. Check that it plays in a logged-out window.
- **X:** the submission post must carry the demo link. If the draft also accepts a video file, attach the video natively too, because native video plays inline in the feed. If it does not, post the native video as the first reply.
- **LinkedIn:** upload the video natively in post 7.

| Time | Beat | On screen | What you say, in short |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 to 0:15 | Hook | One broken quickstart step in red | "Quickstarts break silently. Your users find out first. I built an agent that finds out first." |
| 0:15 to 0:45 | The agent | Architecture diagram, then a sped-up run | Planner, executor in Docker, recovery, clean verification run, ask-once store. |
| 0:45 to 1:25 | neatlogs | Span tree, detection list, Investigate, Claude Code reading the fix over MCP, the numbers table | **Architecture:** every step is a span. **Implementation:** `neatlogs.init`, span kinds. **Runtime:** the live trace. **Reasoning:** detection, then Investigate, then the fix. **Result:** the before and after table. |

| 1:55 to 2:25 | cfo.ai | The Ari model, the Base vs Growth scenario chart, one click on a number's lineage | **Architecture:** cost per run comes from neatlogs. **Implementation:** the prompt to Ari. **Runtime:** a live "what if" question. **Reasoning:** price vs margin. **Result:** price, margin, runway. |
| 2:25 to 2:50 | Recovery and proof | A failed step, the retry, the clean re-run passing | "Here a step failed. Here is what the agent did next. Here is the clean run that proves the fix." |

# FirstRun Brand and Design

Packaging decides the 20% video score and most of the 15% build-in-public score. It also decides the $500 community award, because that award looks at "the quality of the launch and content". This file fixes the look once, so every asset matches without a decision on the day.

## The Name Always Travels With Its Tagline

- **Name:** FirstRun. One word, capital F and capital R.
- **Tagline:** "Your quickstart, run by an agent before your users run it."
- **Short tagline for cards and the video title:** "Docs that work (literally)." It echoes the hackathon track name, "Build an agent that works (literally)", and the judges will recognize the wink.
- **One-sentence pitch:** "FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container like a brand-new developer, and opens a pull request when a step breaks."
- **The word is generic.** GitHub uses "firstrun" for OS setup wizards. Always write "FirstRun" next to "quickstart" or "docs" so search finds it. Repo name: `firstrun`. Hashtag: `#neatHack` only.

## The Visual Language Is Light Mode With Real Logos

**Decision 2026-10-10: every image, diagram, UI and slide is light mode.** The first dark cards were replaced the same day. The product still lives in a terminal, so a terminal window stays as the signature object, drawn light.

1. **Warm off-white page, white cards, soft shadow.**
2. **Green means a step passed. Red means a step broke.** Blue is the accent for links, connectors and the wordmark cursor.
3. **The step counter**, such as `step 4/7`, stays as the signature element.
4. **Real logos for every tool a post names.** The files live in `META/Attachments/neathack/logos/`: `neatlogs.png`, `entire.svg`, `cfoai.svg`. They come from each company's own site. Never redraw or recolor a logo.
5. **No sloppy diagrams.** Connectors are drawn arrows, columns line up on one grid, and every label is real text from the spec.

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Background | `#F6F4EE` | Every card and page background |
| Card | `#FFFFFF` | Nodes, panels, the terminal window |
| Ink | `#14161A` | Body text and headlines |
| Muted | `#5B6470` | Labels, captions |
| Line | `#DAD6CB` | Card borders |
| Pass | `#17803D` | Passed steps, the verified badge |
| Fail | `#C9302C` | Broken steps |
| Accent | `#1B63D6` | Connectors, links, wordmark cursor |

**Type:** Inter 800 for headlines, JetBrains Mono for terminal text, labels and numbers. Both are free on Google Fonts.

**Wordmark:** `FirstRun` in JetBrains Mono 700 with a blue block cursor.

**Sources:** the source HTML for each card sits in `META/Attachments/neathack/cards/<name>/card.html`. Render with the Playwright script at 2x, then read the preview at phone size before it ships.

## Every Screenshot Follows Five Rules

The cards and the video are built from real screenshots, so the screenshots decide the quality.

1. **Terminal:** Windows Terminal, font JetBrains Mono at size 18, a dark theme, a window 120 columns wide. Clear the screen before each capture.
2. **Browser:** zoom to 125% for neatlogs, entire.io and cfo.ai, so text reads on a phone.
3. **Crop to one idea.** A trace screenshot shows the span tree and nothing else.
4. **No secrets.** Hide the API key fields, your email and the browser bookmarks bar.
5. **Save every screenshot** to `D:\Atharva\NOTES\META\Attachments\neathack\` with a name that says what it shows, such as `sat-first-trace.png`. The card skill and the video both pull from there.

## The README Is the Landing Page

Judges open the repo before they watch the video. The README reads like a product page, top to bottom:

1. The wordmark and the tagline.
2. One GIF of a real run: a red step turning into a green verified step, 10 seconds or less.
3. Three badges: `neatHack 2026`, `traced with neatlogs`, `checkpoints by Entire`.
4. The one-sentence pitch.
5. The before and after table with real numbers.
6. "How it works": the architecture diagram.
7. "How each tool is used": one short paragraph each for neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, with links to the evidence.
8. A 5-minute quickstart, proven by FirstRun running on this README.
9. Limits, stated plainly.

Haimantika Mitra owns docs at Entire and Abhi Singh asks whether things survive a real trial. Points 8 and 9 are for them.

## The Architecture Diagram Shows Five Boxes

One diagram, used in the README, the video and post 1. It shows only five boxes:

`Docs page` → `Planner` → `Executor in a clean container` → `Recovery (ask once)` → `Verifier in a fresh container` → `Report and PR`

Below the boxes, one band shows neatlogs tracing every box. The full tool map, with neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai and their logos, is `META/Attachments/neathack/firstrun-tool-map.jpg`, source in `cards/tool-map/`. The README uses a light mermaid version of the same five boxes.
=====

6	# Video Make
7	
8	This skill builds new videos in the video studio. The studio is a clone of
9	[nateherkai/hyperframes-student-kit](https://github.com/nateherkai/hyperframes-student-kit)
10	at `D:/Atharva/video-studio`, pinned to the commit in `scripts/setup.sh`.
11	All tooling, packages and footage live there. The claude-config repo holds only

13	
14	## 1. Start Every Session With the Environment
15	
16	Run this in every Bash call that touches the studio, because the Bash tool
17	drops environment variables between calls:
18	
19	```bash
20	source ~/.claude/skills/video-make/scripts/studio-env.sh
21	```
22	
23	It puts Node 22 and ffmpeg 7.1 first on PATH and sets `$VIDEO_STUDIO`. Without
24	it, the system Node 20 and ImageMagick's ffmpeg 4.2 run, and the kit fails.
25	
26	If anything looks broken, run the doctor first:
27	
28	```bash
29	bash ~/.claude/skills/video-make/scripts/setup.sh --doctor
30	```
31	
32	When the doctor fails, or `$VIDEO_STUDIO` does not exist (a new PC), build the
33	studio yourself before anything else. Do not ask the user how it was set up
34	before, because the script holds all of it:
35	
36	```bash
37	bash ~/.claude/skills/video-make/scripts/setup.sh
38	```
39	
40	It installs any missing fnm, Node 22, ffmpeg and Python with winget, clones the
41	kit at the pinned commit, installs the packages, downloads the render browser
42	and the Whisper model, and ends with a test render. On a new PC it takes about
43	10 minutes. Tell the user it is running, then continue the task.
44	
45	`STUDIO.md` in this folder holds the workspace layout, setup, updates, keys and
46	every known issue. Read it when setup fails or before you change versions.
47	
48	## 2. Read the Kit's Own Sub-Skill, Not the Global One
49	
50	The kit ships 15 sub-skills in `$VIDEO_STUDIO/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`.
51	They name each other as `/hyperframes`, `/gsap`, `/short-form-edit` and so on.
52	Inside this workflow, every such name means the kit file. Read
53	`$VIDEO_STUDIO/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with the Read tool.
54	
55	Do not invoke the global `hyperframes`, `hyperframes-cli` or
56	`hyperframes-registry` skills here. Those are HeyGen's newer docs for the
57	`hyperframes@latest` CLI. The kit pins HyperFrames 0.7.109, and its sub-skills
58	match that version.
59	
60	Kit commands such as `node .claude/skills/cut-silences/scripts/...` and
61	`node scripts/preflight.mjs` run from `$VIDEO_STUDIO`. `npx hyperframes`
62	commands run from the project folder.
63	
64	## 3. Each Request Maps to One Kit Sub-Skill
65	
66	| The user wants | Read this kit sub-skill |
67	| --- | --- |
68	| A video from a concept, script or rough idea | `make-a-video` |
69	| A 10 to 30 second showreel or brand reel cut to music | `motion-showreel` |
70	| A reel, Short or short ad from talking-head footage | `short-form-edit` (do the cuts with video-edit first) |

73	| Motion graphics over a long talking-head edit | `video-storytelling`, then `hyperframes-video-beats` |
74	| Composition rules, captions, TTS, audio-reactive work | `hyperframes` (kit copy) |
75	| GSAP timelines and easing | `gsap` (kit copy) |
76	| Lint, preview, render flags | `hyperframes-cli` (kit copy) |
77	| A catalog block or component | `hyperframes-registry` (kit copy) |

81

93	The kit's files disagree in places. Settle every conflict in this order, which

95

97	   MOTION_PHILOSOPHY's 1.5-second sizzle scenes and a card's 6-second minimum

99	   cards to fit the brief.
100	2. **The kit `hyperframes` sub-skill** wins on code. It overrides the recipes in
101	   `make-a-video`, its `composition-scaffold.md` and MOTION_PHILOSOPHY. Set the
102	   length with `data-duration` on the root, never with an empty
103	   `tl.to({}, {duration})` tween. Mount a sub-composition the way `hyperframes`
104	   shows: a `<template>` wrapper and a `<div>` host.
105	3. **`hyperframes lint` and `hyperframes check`** win over the kit's

113	## 4. One Folder per Video Keeps Footage Out of Git
114	
115	Every video gets one folder: `$VIDEO_STUDIO/video-projects/<slug>/`. The kit's
116	`.gitignore` keeps new project folders, footage and renders out of git.

120	cd "$VIDEO_STUDIO" && npm run new-video -- <slug>
121	```
122	
123	That copies the starter, `DESIGN.md`, `hyperframes.json` and a local
124	`assets/gsap.min.js`. Use it instead of the `npx hyperframes init` that

134	and PNG files that the repo does not ship. Ignore those paths. To start from a whole-scene template, copy
135	`style-templates/<template>/index.html` in, then make these three changes,

139	2. Remove `class="clip"` from any `<video>`. Timed divs carry `clip`, videos do not.

141	
142	## 5. Four Checks and a Preview Run Before Every Render
143	
144	A clean lint does not prove the video looks right, so run all four.
145	
146	```bash
147	source ~/.claude/skills/video-make/scripts/studio-env.sh
148	cd "$VIDEO_STUDIO"
149	node scripts/preflight.mjs video-projects/<slug>
150	cd video-projects/<slug>

153	npx hyperframes preview --background --no-open --port 3002
154	```
155	
156	`hyperframes check` is the only one of these that runs the page. In testing it
157	caught a CSS syntax error that preflight and lint both passed. Do not use
158	`hyperframes validate`: it is deprecated, and it exits 0 even when it prints an
159	error.
160	
161	The fourth check applies only to footage edits:
162	`node scripts/validate-beat-sync.mjs video-projects/<slug>`. It needs

166	Open `http://localhost:3002` in the Browser pane to scrub the timeline.
167	`#project/<slug>?t=10.5` in the URL jumps to a time, but it sometimes opens at

169	`npx hyperframes preview --stop`.
170	
171	To list the timeline durations in the page console, skip the `__proxied` key.
172	`window.__timelines` holds that boolean next to the timelines, and
173	MOTION_PHILOSOPHY's snippet fails on it.
174	
175	When preflight and lint disagree, lint wins. Preflight's
176	`root_data_start_conflicts_with_video` blocker is a false positive on 0.7.109.
177	Lint requires `data-start` on both the root and the `<video>`, and Studio and
178	render both work with it. Verified on 2026-10-02.
179	
180	```bash

182	npx hyperframes render --output renders/final.mp4
183	```
184	
185	A draft of 23 seconds of 1080p footage with one overlay takes about 100 seconds
186	on this laptop. The 8-second starter takes about 45 seconds.
187	
188	## 6. The Encoded MP4 Is What You Verify
189	
190	Inspect the MP4, not the HTML. Extract hero frames and transition frames, look
191	at them, and listen at every audio join:
192	
193	```bash

199	Write what you checked into the project's `VERIFY.md`. Fix every failure

205	2. Name the service and cost before a paid call: Kie.ai for generated footage
206	   or images, ElevenLabs for TTS. Local work needs no approval.
207	3. Never publish or upload a finished video without a direct instruction.

60	## 3. Hard Rules Prevent Silent Failures
61	
62	1. **Confirm the strategy before any cut.** Describe the plan in 4 to 8 plain
63	   sentences and wait for a yes.
64	2. **Never cut inside a word.** In engine A you list what to delete: put each
65	   edge exactly on a word boundary, because `apply-cuts.mjs` deletes any word a
66	   cut overlaps by even 0.02 s. In engine B you list what to keep: pad each edge
67	   30 to 200 ms outward into silence, never into a neighboring word.
68	3. **Word-level transcripts only.** Never SRT or phrase-level output.
69	4. **Never mix timelines.** After a cut, use the retimed transcript that came
70	   with that cut. Raw timestamps against edited footage misplace everything.
71	5. **Transcribe once.** `transcribe.py` caches per source. Use `--force` only
72	   when the source file changed.
73	6. **Subtitles go last** in engine B's filter chain, after every overlay.
74	7. **Engine B keeps 30 ms audio fades** at every segment boundary and extracts
75	   per segment before a lossless concat. `render.py` does both.
76	8. **Verify the rendered file before you show it.** Section 7 lists the checks.

78	## 4. Transcribe With the Unified Script
79	
80	```bash
81	python $S/transcribe.py "$VIDEO_STUDIO/video-projects/<slug>/assets/raw.mp4"
82	python $S/transcribe_batch.py "$VIDEO_STUDIO/video-projects/<slug>/assets"   # many takes
83	python $S/pack_transcripts.py --edit-dir "$VIDEO_STUDIO/video-projects/<slug>"
84	```
85	
86	`--engine auto` (the default) tries ElevenLabs Scribe with each key slot in
87	order. It falls back to local faster-whisper when no key has the Speech to Text
88	permission, which was true for every slot on 2026-10-02. The Whisper path snaps
89	word edges to silences from ffmpeg `silencedetect`, because raw Whisper stretches
90	a word across the pause after it. Whisper `small.en` on CPU transcribed a
91	30-second clip in 15 to 34 seconds. Use `--model medium.en` for hard audio.
92	
93	`transcribe_batch.py` transcribes every video in the folder, so point it at a
94	folder that holds raw takes only, never at `assets/` after a cut.
95	
96	Read `takes_packed.md` first. Each pause of 0.5 s or more starts a new line, so
97	retakes and false starts show up as a line that repeats the line above it.

99	## 5. The Kit Engine Cuts a Talking Head in Three Reviewed Steps
100	
101	Run from `$VIDEO_STUDIO`. Set `P=video-projects/<slug>` first.
102	
103	```bash
104	# 1. Silences. Retimes the transcript onto the cut timeline.
105	node .claude/skills/cut-silences/scripts/cut-silences.mjs $P/transcripts/raw.json \
106	  --video $P/assets/raw.mp4 --out-dir $P/assets --output $P/assets/silenced.mp4 --apply
107	
108	# 2. Mistake candidates on the SILENCED timeline.
109	node .claude/skills/cut-mistakes/scripts/find-cut-candidates.mjs \
110	  $P/assets/raw.silence-transcript.json --out-dir $P/assets
111	```
112	
113	3. Review every candidate in `raw.cut-candidates.md` against the context.
114	   Emphatic repetition ("never, never") is a keep. Then read
115	   `raw.silence-transcript.json` yourself for retakes, every time. The detector
116	   compares pause-separated segments only. In two tests it missed a 10-word and
117	   a 21-word retake, and once it reported 0 candidates. Also read the last line:
118	   a false start of the next section often sits at the tail.
119	   Show the user the proposed cuts, then write the approved list:
120	
121	```json
122	{ "cuts": [ { "start": 5.10, "end": 8.12, "reason": "retake, keep the second take" } ] }
123	```
124	
125	```bash
126	node .claude/skills/cut-mistakes/scripts/apply-cuts.mjs $P/assets/raw.silence-transcript.json \
127	  --cuts $P/assets/approved-cuts.json --video $P/assets/silenced.mp4 \
128	  --out-dir $P/assets --output $P/assets/clean.mp4 --apply
129	```
130	
131	Without `--apply`, `apply-cuts.mjs` writes the transcript and EDL but leaves the old
132	`raw.mistakes-filter.txt` in place. Rendering that filter reuses the previous cuts and gives a
133	byte-identical file. Pass `--apply`, or use `tic_edit.py render`, which builds its own filter.
134	
135	The outputs are `clean.mp4` and `raw.mistakes-transcript.json`. Print the
136	retimed transcript text and read it once, so you catch a word a cut removed.
137	`node scripts/build-edl-review.mjs` builds an HTML page that compares the
138	before and after for the user.
139	
140	To grade or subtitle engine A's result with engine B, register the clean cut
141	as its own source. The kit writes words without a `type` field, which the
142	helpers now read as words.
143	
144	```bash
145	cp $P/assets/raw.mistakes-transcript.json $P/transcripts/clean.json
146	```
147	
148	Then write an EDL with `"sources": {"clean": "assets/clean.mp4"}` and one range
149	from 0 to the clean duration minus 0.05 s. The source key must match the
150	transcript file name, or `render.py` builds 0 subtitle cues and ffmpeg fails.
151	
152	For the motion layer, copy `clean.mp4` to `assets/source.mp4` and
153	`raw.mistakes-transcript.json` to `assets/transcript.json`, then switch to the
154	video-make skill. Its routes `video-storytelling` and `hyperframes-video-beats`
155	cover beats, and its `left-glass-popout` template covers glass cards over
156	footage. For a reel or Short, video-make's `short-form-edit` route takes over
157	from here.

159	## 5b. Tics and Retakes Run Through One Script
160	
161	Use this for a speaker's filler words, stutters and rambling, and for any screen demo going to
162	YouTube. Full measurements, the keep and cut rules, and the traps are in
163	`references/tic-removal.md`. The order never changes:
164	
165	1. Transcribe with `--model medium.en` in the background. While it runs, open the recording's frames to see what is baked in.
166	2. Ask in one `AskUserQuestion`: baked-in captions (re-export without them, edit as is, or hide) and trim depth (light, standard, tight). Do not guess either.
167	3. `python $S/tic_edit.py list $P`, read the packed transcript, write `assets/deletes.json`.
168	4. `build`, `verify`, and `calibrate --apply` only if verify still shows a tic. Then `verify` once more.
169	5. `render`. It writes its own filter with 8 ms fades. Check the duration it prints and the same-size warning.
170	
171	Why a script: Whisper word times for short words are off by 30 to 300 ms, so cuts placed on them
172	leave a "right" behind or clip the word before it. The script places each edge in an audio dip and
173	proves the result by re-transcribing the edited audio. Stop when verify reports only intentional
174	hits ("right now", "as long as you know"). Do not tune further.
175	
176	## 6. Engine B Renders an EDL With Grade and Subtitles
177	
178	Write `edl.json` in the project folder. Sources resolve relative to it, and each
179	source key must match its transcript name:
180	
181	```json
182	{ "version": 1, "sources": {"raw": "assets/raw.mp4"},
183	  "ranges": [ {"source": "raw", "start": 0.0, "end": 5.18, "beat": "HOOK", "reason": "..."} ],
184	  "grade": "warm_cinematic", "subtitles": "master.srt" }
185	```
186	
187	```bash
188	cd "$VIDEO_STUDIO/video-projects/<slug>"
189	python $S/render.py edl.json -o renders/preview.mp4 --preview --build-subtitles
190	python $S/render.py edl.json -o renders/final.mp4 --build-subtitles
191	python $S/grade.py --list-presets
192	```
193	
194	`render.py` extracts each range with the grade and 30 ms fades, concatenates
195	losslessly, builds `master.srt` on the output timeline, burns subtitles last,
196	and normalizes loudness to -14 LUFS. A 23-second, three-range preview took
197	26 seconds. The output keeps the source frame rate (or the EDL's `"fps"`) and
198	orientation, so 9:16 footage stays 9:16. For a Short, raise `MarginV` in
199	`SUB_FORCE_STYLE` to about 90, because the Shorts interface covers the bottom of
200	the frame. Loudness normalization lifted one quiet source by 17 dB. Listen for
201	room noise, and use `--no-loudnorm` when the lift makes noise audible. Pad range edges by 30 to 200 ms around the kept words.
202	
203	`references/craft.md` holds the craft detail: cut technique, the multi-take
204	editor brief, grading, subtitle styles, animation briefs, the EDL fields,
205	session memory and vertical export. Read `references/manim/SKILL.md` before you
206	build a Manim overlay. Build each overlay in its own sub-agent, all in parallel.
207	
208	## 7. Verify the Render Before the User Sees It
209	
210	```bash
211	python $S/timeline_view.py renders/preview.mp4 <cut-1.5> <cut+1.5> -o verify/cut1.png
212	ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 renders/preview.mp4
213	```
214	
215	Keep the window at least 0.1 s inside the file duration, because
216	`timeline_view.py` fails when the end passes the last video frame. For engine A
217	cuts, the cut points on the final timeline are the running sums of the
218	`keep_ranges` durations in `raw.mistakes-edl.json`. Its ranges sit on the
219	silenced timeline, so add the durations rather than reading the start values. Look at every cut boundary in the filmstrip and waveform. Check for a visual
220	jump, a waveform spike (an audio pop), a subtitle hidden by an overlay, and an
221	overlay showing the wrong frames. Also check the first 2 seconds, the last 2
222	seconds and two midpoints. Confirm the duration matches the EDL total. Fix,
223	rerender and recheck, three passes at most, then report what is still wrong.
224

229	the last session in one sentence before asking whether to continue.
230	
231	Deliver the final MP4 path, the EDL or approved cuts, the retimed transcript,
232	and the verification notes. Never upload or publish without a direct instruction.

Do not ask the user to pick assets unless that inventory is missing or unusable. Use the exact required fields from the storyboard and script references.
112	
113	After drafting, run the review loop's plan pass — `../hyperframes-core/references/review-loop.md` § 1: open the board (don't ask whether to), present the plan as a proposal, and ask the two questions — approve or change, and **sketches first** (recommended) or skip. Feedback loops through chat or the board's comments file until approved. This is a **checkpoint gate** (brief contract § 1): in autonomous mode there is no board and nothing to ask — post the same summary as a heads-up and proceed; sketches collapse into the build, and the one preview question comes at Step 6.
114	
115	**Gate:** `STORYBOARD.md` exists, every visual frame has `asset_candidates`, `SCRIPT.md` exists when narration is needed, and the user approved the frame-by-frame plan (autonomous: the summary was posted as a heads-up).
116	
117	---
118	
119	## Step 3.1: Audio
120	
121	Goal: Generate narration, word timings, music, and audio metadata from the approved script.
122	
123	Start audio after Step 3 approval. Run it in the background, then continue to Step 4.
124	
125	**Choose the narration provider and voice from the user's ask before invoking.** Pass the provider selected in Step 0 with `--provider <provider>` (or set `HF_TTS_PROVIDER`). If the request named a voice, gender, or tone, pick a matching voice id and pass it with `--voice <id>`. The pipeline default is otherwise **Marcia (female)** on HeyGen / `am_michael` on Kokoro — so a request like "a male voice" is silently ignored unless you pass the flag. Voice ids are provider-specific; resolve against whichever provider Step 0's sign-in status selected: **HeyGen** (signed in) via `node <MEDIA_DIR>/audio/scripts/heygen-tts.mjs --list` (or `GET /v3/voices?engine=starfish`); **Kokoro** (offline) via the voice table in `<MEDIA_DIR>/audio/references/tts.md` (prefixes `am_`/`bm_` male, `af_`/`bf_` female). When the user expressed no preference, fall back to the remembered voice (brief contract § 2) before the pipeline default, and say which one you used; omit `--voice` only when neither names one. When the user explicitly picked a voice this run, record it (`prefs.mjs record --key voice`).
126	
127	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/audio.mjs --script ./SCRIPT.md --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --hyperframes . --out ./audio_meta.json --provider <provider> --voice <voice-id> &`
128	
129	The audio script handles narration, word timings, BGM lookup from HeyGen's music library, and timing metadata. BGM mood comes from the storyboard's `music:` field; **`music: none` turns BGM off**. This uses the HeyGen Audio API for retrieval, not generation, and uses the same `~/.heygen` credential as TTS. For provider details, read `../media-use/audio/references/tts.md`.
130	
131	If there is no narration and no `SCRIPT.md`, skip voice generation. BGM may still run if the storyboard has a music mood.
132	
133	**The canonical fully-silent marker:** `music: none` in the STORYBOARD.md top YAML block **and** no `SCRIPT.md`. That combination marks the project silent — no narration, no BGM, no SFX. `audio.mjs` recognizes it and generates nothing (it removes any stale `audio_meta.json`; an absent `audio_meta.json` is what assemble treats as silent), so Step 3.1 is a clean skip. Use it when the user asks for a silent / music-free video — don't improvise other spellings.
134	
135	**Gate:** audio job has started, or the project is marked silent (`music: none` + no `SCRIPT.md`).
136	
137	---
138	
139	## Step 4: Frame Visual Design
140	
141	Goal: Add the visual direction, layout intent, and motion choices to each storyboard frame.
142	
143	**Sketch the board first (collaborative only).** The moment the plan is approved, run the sketch pass — `../hyperframes-core/references/review-loop.md` § 2 (don't wait on Step 3.1; sketches don't use timings): wireframe every frame yourself, mark each `built`, pause for the one layout question when the board is full, and revise only the sketches named until the board is confirmed. Stand-ins: plain labeled blocks for the captured assets — the real files arrive with Step 5's workers. Only then write the visual design below onto the confirmed layouts. In autonomous mode, or when the user chose to skip sketches at Step 3, skip this pass — frames go straight from `outline` to `animated` at Step 5.
144	
145	Edit `STORYBOARD.md` in place. Do not create another storyboard. Use `frame.md` as source of truth for color, type, layout feel, and style.
146	
147	Read `references/visual-design.md`, `../hyperframes-animation/blueprints-index.md`, `references/motion-language.md`, and `../hyperframes-animation/rules-index.md`. Use `visual-design.md` for the method (the time-coded shot sequence, the inline Layout vocabulary, and the required `## Video direction` block). Use `../hyperframes-animation/blueprints-index.md` to pick each frame's shot shape. Use `motion-language.md` (the motion vocabulary + the motion doctrine) and `../hyperframes-animation/rules-index.md` (valid rule names) for motion — do not invent motion names.
148	
149	For every visual frame, write a **time-coded shot sequence** into `STORYBOARD.md` per `visual-design.md`'s method: pick the frame's blueprint (or compose), instantiate it with THIS product's content, and pace each Scene's reveal to the voiceover so the frame develops across its full duration instead of front-loading then freezing. State layout and motion **inline** per Scene (vocabularies in `visual-design.md` and `motion-language.md`). Add one video-wide `## Video direction` block.
150	
151	When an element visibly continues across a frame boundary, give both workers the same numerical handoff in `STORYBOARD.md`: add `handoff_out:` to the outgoing frame and a matching `handoff_in:` to the incoming frame. Name the element and its exact x/y position, scale, opacity, and motion direction/speed at the cut — state every field even when it does not change, because a constant is `opacity: 1`, not an omission. Omit the whole block only for a deliberate clean cut. The goal is simple: parallel workers must not invent two different versions of the same seam.
152	
153	Do not change story, script, asset choices, `asset_candidates`, `transition_in`, or captured source material. Do not write HTML in this step.
154	
155	Stage named assets after visual design is locked:
156	
157	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/stage-assets.mjs --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --hyperframes .`
158	
159	**Gate:** every visual frame has a time-coded shot sequence whose reveals are paced to the voiceover (no front-loading); `## Video direction` exists; `assets/` contains the named assets. Collaborative: the sketch board was confirmed.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## Step 5: Build Frames
164	
165	Goal: Build every storyboard frame as an HTML composition and assemble the playable video.
166	
167	Wait for Step 3.1 audio to finish if audio was started. Then sync durations and fetch SFX; skip both if silent.
168	
169	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/audio.mjs sync-durations --audio-meta ./audio_meta.json --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md`
170	
171	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/audio.mjs fetch-sfx --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --hyperframes .`
172	
173	Duration sync is mechanical: real voice duration wins; silent frames keep estimates; never hand-edit synced durations.
174	
175	Check the music against the final cut before assembly. A library track can match the requested mood but open on a quiet build that drains the first seconds of a short launch video. Compare the opening with later five-second sections; when a later section has a stronger, musically clean start, trim from there and keep a short fade-in plus a longer fade-out. If frame or narration timing changes, redo this check against the new final duration so the music never ends early or leaves silence at the tail.
176	
177	Before dispatch, read `../hyperframes-core/references/subagent-dispatch.md`. Build the per-frame packets and the worker role payload:
178	
179	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/frame-packets.mjs --project "$PROJECT_DIR" --storyboard "$PROJECT_DIR/STORYBOARD.md"`
180	
181	The builder writes one bounded packet per frame under `.hyperframes/frame-packets/` (the frame's exact storyboard block + the blueprint body + every cited rule recipe, inlined) and `_role.md` (`../hyperframes-core/references/frame-worker-core.md` + this skill's `sub-agents/frame-worker.md`, concatenated verbatim — the complete worker role). Dispatch one sub-agent per frame, in parallel if possible; otherwise run workers in waves. Each worker gets exactly one frame: its prompt carries `_role.md` and that frame's packet — paste both in full, or hand the two file paths for the worker to read first (equivalent; the worker starts from exactly those two documents either way) — plus a dispatch context with `PROJECT_DIR`, `frame_id`, whether the frame has a **confirmed sketch** on disk (the worker dresses that layout rather than redrawing it — frame-worker core § When a confirmed sketch exists), canvas size, and caption status + keep-out band if captions are enabled.
182	
183	Workers read only their packet and `frame.md`; they never open `STORYBOARD.md` or the skill documents (the packet inlines what was selected upstream). Each worker writes only `compositions/frames/NN-*.html`. Workers must never edit `STORYBOARD.md`.
184	
185	**Full-bleed backgrounds ride on a `class="clip"` layer, never the `#root`.** A frame's ground (color field / gradient / grid) is its own full-duration background clip — a `background` set on the `#root` / `data-composition-id` element is clip-gated to the frame's window and is not a dependable ground, so dark content can land on the black host `body` and render invisible. The video's base ground is painted by the assembler from `frame.md`'s `canvas` color onto the index `#root`. (Full rule + self-check: `../hyperframes-core/references/frame-worker-core.md`.)
186	
187	As each worker returns, the orchestrator marks that frame as `animated` in `STORYBOARD.md`.
188	
189	After audio timings exist, build captions in the background and assemble the index:
190	
191	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/captions.mjs build --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --audio-meta ./audio_meta.json --hyperframes . --out ./caption_groups.json &`
192	
193	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/assemble-index.mjs --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --hyperframes .`
194	
195	`captions.mjs` uses the project's `.hyperframes/caption-skin.html` (copied in Step 2) as the caption look, injecting brand tokens from `frame.md`; with no skin present it renders the built-in default pill. `captions: skipped (<reason>)` is valid. Continue without captions when explicitly skipped.
196	
197	**Gate:** every frame is marked `animated` (collaborative: the sketch board was confirmed at Step 4), `index.html` exists, and captions are built or explicitly skipped.
198	
199	---
200	
201	## Step 6: Finalize
202	
203	Goal: Verify the assembled video, get user approval, and render the final MP4.
204	
205	Inject transitions, run checks, pause for review, then render.
206	
207	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/transitions.mjs inject --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --hyperframes .`
208	
209	`node <SKILL_DIR>/scripts/transitions.mjs verify --storyboard ./STORYBOARD.md --index ./index.html`
210	
211	`npx hyperframes lint`
212	
213	`npx hyperframes check`
214	
215	`npx hyperframes snapshot --at <frame-midpoints-and-each-cut-minus-0.1s-and-plus-0.2s>`
216	
217	`snapshot` stitches the captured frames into one contact sheet (`snapshots/contact-sheet.jpg`). Inspect the midpoint frames for layout failures, then compare the two images around every cut. A continuing element must keep the promised position, scale, opacity, and direction; fix any visible pop before rendering.
218	
219	If a command fails, surface stderr and stop — don't pile on recovery commands. Fix it yourself: the cheapest safe edit to `compositions/frames/NN-*.html`, then rerun the failed check.
220	
221	After checks pass, pause for user review — the review loop's final look (`../hyperframes-core/references/review-loop.md` § 4): one question, on the Studio that has been open since Step 3 — render now, or what changes? (Autonomous: the one kept question, preview first or render.) Then deliver the MP4 with the contact sheet and the frame ids so revisions can target a single frame.
222	
223	Preview: `npx hyperframes preview --background`
224	
225	Render only after user approval (autonomous mode: after the preview-or-render question):
226	
227	`npx hyperframes render --skill=product-launch-video --quality high --output renders/video.mp4`
228	
229	Do not rerun `lint`, `check`, or `snapshot` after rendering unless the user asks.
230	
231	**Gate:** `lint` and `check` passed and the snapshots were inspected before render; user approved at the review pause (autonomous: checks passed and the delivery includes the contact sheet); `renders/video.mp4` exists. Final reply states MP4 path and final duration.
232	
233	---
234	
235	## Quick Reference
236	
237	**Formats:** landscape `1920x1080`; portrait `1080x1920`; square `1080x1080` — derived from the destination (brief contract § 2). Set the format once in the storyboard frontmatter.
238	
239	**Background scripts:** the workflow ships only these scripts under `scripts/`: `build-frame` for adopting + brand-remixing a frame preset into `frame.md` (+ caption skin); `audio` for TTS, transcription, BGM, SFX, and duration syncing; `captions`; `transitions` for inject and verify; `stage-assets` for copying frame-named assets into `assets/`; and `assemble-index`. Everything else is handled by the `hyperframes` CLI.

---
type: Identity Profile
title: "Runtime Contract"
description: "The load order for every writing job, and the checks that run after."
created: 2026-08-22
updated: 2026-09-25
---

# Runtime Contract

> **Purpose:** This file says which rules load, in what order, and which checks run at the end.
> It is the only file that answers "what was applied to this draft". Read it first, every time.
> Adapted from the runtime contract in [Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer](https://github.com/Deupaxx/EveryDay-Writer).
> The architecture is theirs. The rules and the voice are mine.

## Always loaded

Six files load for every piece of writing, on every channel, in this order.

1. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`, this file. The load order and the checks.
2. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md`. The failure patterns a regex cannot see.
3. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/write-simply.md`. The plain style, and the test for whether the ideas are right.
4. `DIGITAL TWIN/World.md`. The villain, the vision, and what the piece is for.
5. `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. The bar the insight clears before a word is drafted.
6. `DIGITAL TWIN/Voice.md`. How the writing sounds.

Files 2 and 3 are a pair. The pattern rules say what to remove, and `write-simply.md` says what to
aim for, so a draft that only obeys the first one reads stripped.

`World.md` decides what the piece argues and `Voice.md` decides how it sounds, so the two never
collide. Name the skill-tree node before you draft a line. A piece that advances no node is an
idea, so send it back to `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS/`.

`net-new-value.md` is the guiding principle for all content, on every channel. Write the core
insight as one sentence and name its box before you draft. Only box 4 ships: non-obvious to the
reader and tactical enough to use today. A piece outside box 4 gets one upgrade, then goes back to
the idea bank.

`SCRIPTS/slop/slop_rules.py` holds the banned words, phrases and punctuation. `DIGITAL TWIN/rules/`
holds the prose rules, one file each. The `core` rules load into every session through the generated
block in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so you never copy them into another file.

The `craft` rules load for every writing job. Run this once per session before the first draft:

```bash
python SCRIPTS/slop/rules_prompt.py --profile craft
```

## Loaded on demand

One more file loads, chosen by the job. Never load two.

| The job | Load this |
|---|---|
| A Substack article, an essay, a long piece | `DIGITAL TWIN/Long-Form Writing Rules.md` |
| A tutorial, a how-to, a README, developer docs | `DIGITAL TWIN/Technical Writing Style Guide.md` |
| A LinkedIn post, a Note, a tweet, a caption | nothing extra. The channel skill carries it |

`DIGITAL TWIN/AI Writing Policy.md` outranks all of the above and it changes rarely, so read it
when you start a writing session and not once per draft.

title: FirstRun demo video shot sheet
